examInfo.format: Many states test new life and health agents with one combined exam that has a general knowledge portion and a state law portion. This site follows the Pearson VUE Life and Health General Knowledge outline used in Texas (effective September 1, 2026): 100 scored questions, 50 on life insurance and 50 on health insurance, plus 10 unscored pretest questions. In Texas the full General Lines Life, Accident and Health exam also has a 30-question state section and allows 150 minutes in total. The 100-minute timer here is this site's practice setting for the general portion only. Mock exams here use 4 answer choices with one correct answer, and practice sets show 2, 3, or 4 choices by level. All questions on this site are original AI practice questions, and the state law portion is not covered.

passCriteria.description: Each state sets its own passing score. In Texas the exam is scored as a whole (general and state parts together) and reported on a scale where 70 is passing; the scaled score is not a percentage. This site uses 70% correct as a practice goal only.

content.eligibility: Each state sets its own rules for a life and health (or life, accident and health) agent license, such as minimum age, pre-license education, fingerprints, and how to apply after you pass. Check your state department of insurance before you register.
content.intro: The life and health insurance license exam checks that a new agent understands the products they will sell and the rules for selling them honestly. The general knowledge portion has two halves. The life half covers whole life, term, universal and variable life, annuities, policy riders and provisions, the application and underwriting, and retirement and tax topics. The health half covers disability income, medical expense plans, Medicare supplement and long-term care, mandatory health policy provisions, Medicare, Medicaid and Social Security, and field underwriting. Short practice sets here let you study one chapter at a time, and a mock exam puts 100 questions together.
content.trendSummary: In the Texas outline, the life half has 50 questions: types of policies 15, riders, provisions, options and exclusions 15, the application, underwriting and delivery 12, and retirement and other concepts 8. The health half also has 50: types of policies 16, policy provisions, clauses and riders 15, field underwriting 8, social insurance 6, and other insurance concepts 5. Policy types and policy provisions together make up 61 of the 100 questions.
content.studyTip: Learn the products first, because provision and underwriting questions assume you know how each policy works. Then study the provisions side by side, since life and health policies both have a grace period, reinstatement, and incontestable clause but with different details. Finish with Medicare, Medicaid, Social Security, and tax rules.

faqs.question: How many questions are on the general knowledge portion?
faqs.answer: In the Texas outline it has 100 scored questions, 50 on life and 50 on health, plus 10 unscored pretest questions. The state law section is separate; in Texas it has 30 scored questions plus 5 pretest questions.

faqs.question: What score do I need to pass?
faqs.answer: Each state sets its own passing score. Texas reports a scaled score where 70 passes, based on the whole exam, and the scaled score is not a percentage. Check your state's candidate handbook for the exact rule.

faqs.question: Does this site cover my state's insurance laws?
faqs.answer: No. This site covers only the general product knowledge portion. Study your state's insurance code, licensing rules, and marketing rules separately for the state portion.

faqs.question: Can I retake the exam if I fail?
faqs.answer: Rules differ by state. The Texas handbook says a candidate who failed can schedule a new exam within one day, with no limit on the number of attempts, but each attempt has a fee.

faqs.question: Are these real exam questions?
faqs.answer: No. Real exam questions are kept secret by the test vendor. All questions here are original practice questions written from the public content outline.

studyTips.studyOrder: Start with the two largest areas: Types of Life Policies and Annuities (15 of the 100 questions in the outline) and Types of Health Policies (16). Then study the provisions chapters for each half, which have 15 questions each, because they assume you already know the products. Finish with underwriting, retirement and tax rules, and Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security.
studyTips.hardChapters: Health Policy Provisions, Clauses, and Riders is hard because it is full of time limits, such as 20 days for notice of claim, 90 days for proof of loss, and 31 days of grace for most premium modes, that are easy to mix up. In the life half, nonforfeiture options and beneficiary rules are often confused. Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security together have only 6 of the 100 questions in the outline, but for Medicare you must match each service to the right part.
studyTips.examDay: In Texas the full General Lines Life, Accident and Health exam allows 150 minutes for 100 general and 30 state scored questions plus 15 unscored pretest questions, so check the time on your own state's handbook. Read every word of story questions, because words such as except, always, and primary often decide the answer. Pretest questions are mixed in and cannot be identified, so answer every question carefully.
